query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is primarily controlled by the formation of an adherent, continuous oxide layer that reduces friction and plastic deformation during sliding wear.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating deposited onto a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal pre-oxidation treatment (anneal in air at 600°C for 1 hour) to deliberately develop a uniform oxide scale prior to wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted between 600°C and 800°C under loads typical of high-temperature protective applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous oxide scale—likely enriched in Cr and Fe oxides—that forms on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a protective barrier that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact and plastic deformation, thereby reducing friction and abrasive wear. This layer modifies the contact mechanics during high-temperature sliding by providing a lubricious, stable surface that resists further degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, pre-oxidized coatings will exhibit significantly lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates (e.g., shallower wear tracks and less debris formation) compared to the as-deposited baseline coatings, thanks to the protective oxide film.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate within the high-temperature range of 600°C to 800°C under high-load sliding wear conditions relevant to protective coatings. At lower temperatures or very high loads where oxide stability may be compromised, other mechanisms might dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the long-term stability of the oxide layer under cyclic wear conditions and the possibility of oxide spallation at the upper temperature limits, as well as the exact load dependence on wear behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on identical metal substrates. Subject one set to thermal pre-oxidation (annealing in air at 600°C for 1 hour) to promote oxide scale formation, while leaving the other set as-deposited. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests at about 700°C under the same applied load. Characterize the resulting wear behavior using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) for oxide characterization, surface profilometry to measure wear track depth, and friction coefficient measurements.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per sliding distance)
Surface oxide layer integrity and thickness (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not demonstrate a significant reduction in wear rate, lower friction, and improved oxide layer stability (relative to the as-deposited baseline) under the designated high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis—that the oxide layer is the dominant factor governing wear resistance at high temperatures—must be rejected.
